### 2.1 Fast Calorimeter Simulation Challenge 2022 (calochallenge-2022)

`data/benchmarks/physics/calochallenge-2022.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-10-14

*Generative surrogates for Geant4 calorimeter showers on four datasets, scored on fidelity, generation time and size.*

A community challenge, announced in February 2022, for deep generative models that stand in for Geant4 in simulating calorimeter showers, the costliest part of LHC detector simulation. Entrants learn the distribution of voxelised energy deposits given the incident particle's energy, from Geant4 showers on three datasets: dataset 1, photons (368 voxels) and charged pions (533 voxels) simulated in the ATLAS calorimeter and taken from ATLAS open data; and datasets 2 and 3, electrons in an idealised silicon-tungsten calorimeter simulated with Geant4's Par04 example, at 6,480 and 40,500 voxels. Each dataset has training and evaluation files, all public on Zenodo under CC BY 4.0. Entrants sent files of generated showers, and the organisers compared them with the Geant4 evaluation file through separation powers of high-level feature histograms, binary classifiers' AUCs, a multiclass classifier's log-posterior across all submissions, FPD and KPD, and precision, recall, density and coverage. Each model's generation was timed in a container on one cluster, at three batch sizes, beside its parameter count. No aggregate is formed and no winner was declared. The write-up (Reports on Progress in Physics 88, 116201) compares 59 submissions from 31 models by 23 collaborations, and the datasets, submitted samples, evaluation script and result tables stay public as a benchmark.

#### calochallenge-2022 · Identity and id

- `self_description` · [S1][calochallenge-2022-s1]

#### calochallenge-2022 · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary physics/simulation-surrogates; secondary physics/particle-physics · [S3][calochallenge-2022-s3]
  - why: Entrants are generative models that stand in for Geant4's calorimeter simulation and are scored against held-out Geant4 showers, which is simulation-surrogates' definition. The physical subject is the response of particle detectors to single particles, so particle-physics is secondary; that leaf's definition, analysing collision or detector data to recover physics quantities, does not cover generating detector data, which is why it is not primary (see review\_checks).
  > we are interested in surrogate models that are faithful (i.e. reproduce the showers of Geant4 as close as possible)
- `capability` = scientific-prediction · [S3][calochallenge-2022-s3]
  - why: The challenge's claim is that a model learns the distribution of a physical system's state, the energy deposited in each calorimeter voxel given the incident energy, and every quality metric compares the generated showers with Geant4's reference computation on a held-out file. What is predicted is a distribution, sampled, rather than one state per input (see review\_checks).
  > participants were tasked with training their favorite generative model on the provided calorimeter shower datasets
- `evaluation_method` = statistical-fit, classification-metric, entrant-relative-ranking · [S3][calochallenge-2022-s3]
  - why: The write-up reports its metrics per dataset, each apart. statistical-fit for the separation powers between histograms of high-level features (energy per layer, total energy, centres of energy and their widths, sparsity), a normalised chi-squared-type distance; for FPD and KPD, Frechet and kernel distances computed on the same features; for the layer-energy correlations; and for precision, recall, density and coverage, nearest-neighbour statistics of the generated and reference samples. classification-metric for the binary classifiers' AUC: a network is trained afresh to tell each submission from the Geant4 file, so the AUC is a statistic of scores against a labelled key, not the output of a fixed scoring model. entrant-relative-ranking for the multiclass test: one classifier is trained on all submissions together and read on the Geant4 sample, so the log-posterior of every submission moves when one is added or removed.
  > For each of these observables, we compute the separation power between the submissions and the held-out test set.
- `designed_for_subjects` = scientific-surrogate-model · [S1][calochallenge-2022-s1]
  - why: The entrants are deep generative models (GANs, VAEs, normalising flows, diffusion and flow-matching models) trained to stand in for Geant4 and scored against its showers.
  > Therefore there is an urgent need to develop GEANT4 emulators that are both fast (computationally lightweight) and accurate.
- `secondary_axes` = latency, throughput · [S3][calochallenge-2022-s3]
  - why: Generation time is reported beside quality at batch size 1, the way Geant4 simulates, and at 100 and 10,000, on CPU and GPU, with the trainable parameter count as a proxy for memory.
  > We therefore study batch sizes of 1, 100, and 10 000 to show how the models behave under different use cases.

Considered and rejected:

- `capability` not `distribution-shift-generalization` · [S1][calochallenge-2022-s1]
  - why: The site listed an interpolation test, one incident energy left out of training and generated after it, among the planned metrics, but the write-up reports no such test; every dataset is scored on an evaluation file drawn like its training file.
  > Interpolation capabilities: leave out one energy in training and generate samples at that energy after training.
- `evaluation_method` not `composite` · [S1][calochallenge-2022-s1]
  - why: No published figure combines the metrics. Quality, generation time and model size are reported apart and compared on Pareto fronts, and the organisers expected no single winner.
  > It is expected that there will not necessarily be a single clear winner, but different methods will have their pros and cons.
- `evaluation_method` not `model-derived-metric` · [S3][calochallenge-2022-s3]
  - why: The classifiers are trained afresh for each evaluation, ten per submission and averaged, not released as fixed scoring models, which the term's exclusion leaves to the final statistic's method. FPD and KPD are computed on the physics features themselves, not on a network's activations as FID is.
  > We train ten classifiers with different random initialization and average the AUCs when reporting the results.

**Open review checks** (7):

1. (field `domain.primary`) Primary domain. simulation-surrogates' definition fits verbatim, and the fair-universe entry rejected that leaf only because no emulator was scored against its simulator. But the surrogates/fluid-dynamics distinction says a benchmark with one physical system as its subject takes that subject's leaf whatever the method. If calorimeter showers count as one system (two detectors, three particle types), particle-physics would be primary, though its definition (analysing detector data to recover physics quantities) does not describe generating showers. · [S3][calochallenge-2022-s3]
   > we are interested in surrogate models that are faithful (i.e. reproduce the showers of Geant4 as close as possible)
2. (field `capability`) scientific-prediction is assigned to models that sample a distribution of showers rather than predict one state per input; generation-fidelity is the alternative, kept out only by its exclusion test.
3. (field `evaluation_method`) Evaluation methods. The AUC comes from a classifier trained afresh on each submission against Geant4, so it is filed as classification-metric although the entrant classifies nothing. entrant-relative-ranking rests on the multiclass log-posterior alone, one of several published figures with no headline. Precision, recall, density and coverage are nearest-neighbour manifold statistics, put under statistical-fit although classification-metric names precision and recall. Separation power could be read as domain-metric. · [S3][calochallenge-2022-s3]
   > When evaluating the trained classifier on a Geant4-based test set, we can read off which submission the Geant4 sample is closest to.
4. (field `governance.submission_process`) sandboxed-rerun is set for the timings only (organisers ran each group's container); the quality scores come from submitted samples. How samples were sent to the organisers is not described in the sources read. · [S3][calochallenge-2022-s3]
   > each submitting group created a singularity container
5. (field `lifecycle`) lifecycle active rests on one 2026 paper using datasets 2 and 3. With the challenge closed and its record final, mature (an ended competition whose instrument stays in use) is the alternative. activity closed has no dated close.
6. (field `subsets`) Identity. The entry is the 2022 challenge with its four datasets as subsets. The Par04 datasets with varying incident angles, published beside datasets 2 and 3 but outside the challenge, are not included; a later CaloChallenge, if one runs, would be an edition here or an entry of its own. · [S4][calochallenge-2022-s4]
   > Although samples with varying incident angles are available, only perpendicular incidence is considered here.
7. (field `data.contamination_risk`) contamination\_risk medium because the evaluation files are public beside the training files; no source considers training on them.

### 2.2 AirfRANS (airfrans)

`data/benchmarks/physics/airfrans.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-10-14

*1,000 RANS simulations of subsonic airfoil flow, for learned surrogates of the flow fields and the drag and lift.*

A dataset and benchmark of 1,000 two-dimensional, incompressible, steady-state Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes simulations of subsonic flow around airfoils from the NACA 4- and 5-digit series, at Reynolds numbers of 2 to 6 million and angles of attack of -5 to 15 degrees, computed with OpenFOAM's simpleFoam solver and the k-omega SST turbulence model on meshes of 250,000 to 300,000 cells. A learned surrogate receives the mesh nodes with the inlet velocity, the distance to the airfoil and the surface normals, and predicts the velocity, pressure and turbulent viscosity at every node; the drag and lift coefficients are computed from the predicted fields. Four tasks split the simulations: full data (800 training, 200 test), scarce data (200 training, the same test set), and Reynolds-number and angle-of-attack extrapolation, whose test simulations lie outside the training ranges. Models are scored by the MSE of each field in the volume and on the airfoil, by the relative error of the drag and lift coefficients, and by Spearman's rank correlation between predicted and true coefficients, which the authors put first for design use. The baselines are an MLP, GraphSAGE, PointNet and Graph U-Net; the June 2023 arXiv version discloses that the main text's baselines were trained with a plain MSE loss rather than the paper's volume-plus-surface loss, and adds results for the latter. AirfRANS has no leaderboard of its own. IRT SystemX ran two Codabench competitions on it, in 2023-2024 and at NeurIPS 2024 (ML4CFD, with the AirfRANS authors among the organisers), with their own split and a global score that adds physical compliance and speed-up; both have closed.

#### airfrans · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary physics/fluid-dynamics; secondary physics/simulation-surrogates · [S1][airfrans-s1]
  - why: The one physical system is subsonic turbulent flow around a 2D airfoil, and every score is on predicted flow fields or the forces derived from them. The taxonomy sends a surrogate benchmark with one physical system as its subject to that subject's leaf, with simulation-surrogates (the method) secondary; PDEBench and the Well are primary simulation-surrogates because they span many systems.
  > we develop AIRFRANS, a dataset for studying the two-dimensional incompressible steady-state Reynolds-Averaged Navier–Stokes equations over airfoils
- `capability` = scientific-prediction · [S1][airfrans-s1]
  - why: A model predicts the velocity, pressure and turbulent viscosity fields of a simulated flow, and the forces on the airfoil, and is scored against the RANS solver's solution.

- `capability` = distribution-shift-generalization · [S1][airfrans-s1]
  - why: The Reynolds and angle-of-attack tasks train on the middle of each parameter's range and test on simulations outside it, scored as tasks of their own; the predicted fields and the metrics are unchanged, only the inputs move.

- `capability` = sample-efficiency · [S1][airfrans-s1]

- `evaluation_method` = statistical-fit · [S1][airfrans-s1]
  - why: Every metric is a general error or correlation statistic against the simulated values, the MSE of each field, the relative error of the drag and lift coefficients, and Spearman's rank correlation of those coefficients.

**Open review checks** (5):

1. (field `events`) Identity. The two Codabench competitions are recorded as events of this entry, which makes activity closed and puts the route in history. They have their own split (103/200/496), a composite global score with physics and speed-up criteria, a private final test set and IRT SystemX as lead organiser, so the NeurIPS 2024 ML4CFD competition could be an entry of its own; AirfRANS's activity would then be no-submission-channel. · [S3][airfrans-s3]
   > this iteration centers on a task fundamental to a well-established physical application: airfoil design simulation, utilizing our proposed AirfRANS dataset
2. (field `domain.primary`) Domain. Primary fluid-dynamics follows the taxonomy's rule for a surrogate benchmark with one physical system; PDEBench and the Well are primary simulation-surrogates because they span many. engineering-design was rejected because the scored artefact is a prediction, although the paper calls the dataset design-oriented.
3. (field `capability`) sample-efficiency rests on the scarce task's fixed 200-simulation training budget scored as a task of its own; the paper frames it as a data regime, and the full task's 800 is also a fixed budget. · [S1][airfrans-s1]
   > We choose to only run 1000 simulations as one of the goals of this dataset is to be close to real-world settings, i.e. limited quantity of data
4. (field `governance.maintainer_type`) maintainer\_type industry-lab rests on the repositories' GitHub organisation (Extrality, now named SimAI and linked to Ansys) and on the competition paper's affiliations; no quoted source states the organisation's ownership. The data is on Sorbonne's ISIR server, so academic-lab is the alternative.
5. (field `aggregation_policy`) Smaller calls. aggregation\_policy none-by-design is read from the paper's metrics hierarchy, which no source calls a policy. contamination\_risk is medium where PDEBench and the Well chose unknown. released is the arXiv date although the data was public from August 2022, and the paper calls its ICLR 2022 workshop dataset (UIUC airfoils, coarser meshes) the first version of this one, which is not recorded as a version.

### 2.3 FAIR Universe HiggsML Uncertainty Challenge (fair-universe-higgsml)

`data/benchmarks/physics/fair-universe-higgsml.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-11-24

*Confidence intervals on the Higgs signal strength under six systematic uncertainties, scored on coverage and width.*

A NeurIPS 2024 competition and dataset from the FAIR Universe project, led by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. Each scored item is a pseudo-experiment, an unlabelled set of simulated proton-proton collisions (H to tau tau signal against Z, ttbar and diboson backgrounds, generated with Pythia 8.2 and Delphes 3.5.0, 28 features per event) drawn with a randomised signal strength mu and six nuisance parameters for systematic effects such as the tau and jet energy scales and the background normalisations. A submission is code (a model.py with fit and predict) that receives the labelled training set and a biasing script, and returns a 68.27% confidence interval for mu on each pseudo-experiment. The Quantile Score rewards narrow intervals and penalises coverage away from 68.27%, more heavily for under-coverage. Codabench ran the code on organiser hardware at NERSC and LBNL from August 2024 to March 2025; every submission was then re-run on pseudo-experiments from a private 120M-event set, and HEPHY (Vienna) and IBRAHIME (UIUC) were declared joint first. The public dataset has been on Zenodo under CC BY 4.0 since 2025 as a long-term benchmark, with no submission route open. FAIR Universe's 2025 and 2026 NeurIPS challenges are on weak lensing, a different task, and are not included here.

### 2.4 TrackML Particle Tracking Challenge (trackml)

`data/benchmarks/physics/trackml.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-10-14

*Grouping simulated LHC detector hits into particle tracks, in a 2018 Kaggle accuracy phase and a Codalab speed phase.*

A two-phase data challenge on charged-particle track reconstruction, run in 2018 and 2019 by tracking experts from the ATLAS, CMS and LHCb experiments with machine-learning researchers and ChaLearn. Each event is a simulated proton-proton bunch crossing under High-Luminosity LHC conditions (a ttbar hard scatter with 200 soft interactions overlaid, generated with Pythia 8 and propagated through a virtual silicon tracker with the ACTS fast simulation): about 100,000 3D hits that the entrant must partition into tracks, one per charged particle, some 10,000 per event. The score is the weighted fraction of hits assigned to the right track. A track counts only when more than half its hits come from one particle and it holds more than half of that particle's hits; weights favour a track's first and last hits and high-momentum particles; a perfect solution scores 1 and a random one 0. The Accuracy phase ran on Kaggle from 30 April to 13 August 2018 (651 teams) on 125 test events whose hits were released and whose truth was held back, 36 for the public leaderboard and 89 for the final ranking. The Throughput phase ran on Codalab from September 2018 to March 2019 on a corrected dataset: entrants uploaded code that the organisers ran on undisclosed events on two CPU cores, and the score combined the accuracy with the mean time per event (seven entrants scored). Both phases are closed. Each phase's training data is on Zenodo under CC BY 4.0, and the Kaggle data is still a standard benchmark for learned tracking, usually in a reduced pixel-only setting with its own efficiency metrics.

#### trackml · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary physics/particle-physics · [S1][trackml-s1]
  - why: The scored output is the grouping of a collision event's detector hits into the trajectories of the particles that left them, recovered from simulated detector data, which is the leaf's definition. FAIR Universe HiggsML, the family's own particle-physics example, is the same kind of LHC-simulation challenge.
  > Given 100.000 points, the participants had to connect them into about 10.000 arcs of circles, following the trajectory of particles issued from very high energy proton collisions
- `capability` = perception · [S1][trackml-s1]
  - why: The input is an unordered cloud of about 100,000 3D detector hits per event, with the detector cells behind each, and the score measures the track structure recovered from it. PLAsTiCC's entry rejected the term for tabulated photometry; IceCube's assigned it for a cloud of detector hits, as here.
  > Each hit is a 3D measurement in Cartesian coordinates
- `capability` = scientific-prediction · [S1][trackml-s1]
  - why: Systems reconstruct which hits each charged particle left along its trajectory, a state of the simulated collision recovered from measurements of it, and the score compares it with the simulation's truth. The track parameters themselves are out of scope (see review\_checks).
  > listing for each event the measured 3D points, and the list of 3D points associated to a true track
- `evaluation_method` = domain-metric · [S1][trackml-s1]
  - why: The TrackML score is defined for this challenge from tracking practice. Tracks and particles are matched by the double-majority rule, hits are weighted by their place on the track and the particle's transverse momentum, and the matched weights are summed per event and averaged over events. The paper finds it consistent with the physics reconstruction metrics.
  > This score is largely consistent with the various and more complicated metrics used in physics reconstruction
- `designed_for_subjects` = domain-specialist-model · [S1][trackml-s1]

The jury prizes went to a Hough-transform-like method with a boosted-tree classifier, a DBSCAN-based method and an LSTM track follower; the runner-up was a dense network predicting which hit pairs share a track.

- `task` = exists true; input one simulated event: about 100,000 hits, each a 3D position with its detector volume, layer and module, and the detector cells behind it, for training only: the per-hit truth (the generating particle, its true position and momentum at the hit, and the hit's score weight) and the particles' initial parameters; output A track identifier for every hit of every event, each hit in exactly one track. Deriving the track parameters is not part of the task.; scoring The TrackML score. Tracks and particles are matched by the double-majority rule (more than half of the track's hits from one particle, and more than half of that particle's hits in the track), and each matched track contributes the summed weights of its correct hits. Weights favour a track's first and last hits and high-momentum particles, are zero for noise and very short tracks, and sum to one per event; event scores are averaged. In the Throughput phase this accuracy, which had to reach 0.5, was combined with the mean time per event, capped at 600 s, into an unbounded score, and secondary particles were left out of the accuracy.; tests_hidden_from_system true · [S5][trackml-s5]

### 2.5 PLAsTiCC (plasticc)

`data/benchmarks/physics/plasticc.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-10-14

*Classifying 3.5 million simulated LSST light curves into 15 classes, scored by weighted log loss (Kaggle, 2018).*

A data challenge, run on Kaggle from 28 September to 17 December 2018 by a team from the LSST Dark Energy Science Collaboration and the Transients and Variable Stars Science Collaboration, to classify astronomical transients and variables from light curves simulated to look like three years of the Rubin Observatory's LSST survey. Each object comes as fluxes over time in six passbands with host-galaxy redshift and Milky Way extinction metadata. A classifier trained on 7,848 labelled objects must give every one of about 3.5 million test objects a probability for each of 15 classes: 14 seen in training and a class 99 for objects of none of them, which hides four simulated types never shown in training. The training set is deliberately unrepresentative, brighter and nearer than the test set, as a spectroscopically confirmed sample would be. Scoring is a multi-class log loss that averages each class over its own objects and up-weights rare classes, so every class counts about equally; the weights were hidden during the competition. Kaggle scored a third of the test set on the public leaderboard and ranked the prizes on the other two thirds. The test labels were released on Zenodo in January 2019 under CC BY 4.0, and the data are still used to train and test classifiers.

#### plasticc · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary physics/astrophysics-cosmology · [S1][plasticc-s1]
  - why: The scored quantity is the astronomical class of a source, inferred from its photometric time series and host-galaxy metadata. The observations are simulated to mimic LSST's.
  > how well can we classify astronomical transients and variables from a simulated light curve data set designed to mimic the data from LSST
- `capability` = scientific-prediction · [S1][plasticc-s1]
  - why: A classifier predicts which kind of astrophysical object, from supernova types to RR Lyrae and AGN, produced each light curve, and is scored against the class the simulation drew.
  > how well can we classify objects in the sky that vary in brightness from simulated LSST time-series data
- `capability` = calibration-uncertainty · [S3][plasticc-s3]
  - why: Entrants submit a probability for every class of every object, and the log loss scores those probabilities, not a hard label.
  > For each object, you must submit a set of predicted probabilities (one for every category)
- `capability` = distribution-shift-generalization · [S4][plasticc-s4]
  - why: The training set is built as a mock spectroscopic sample, brighter and at lower redshift than the test set, and the score is computed on the shifted test set. Class 99 adds a second shift, four object types absent from training (see review\_checks).
  > the PLAsTiCC training set is non-representative by design
- `evaluation_method` = uncertainty-calibration-score · [S3][plasticc-s3]
  - why: The metric is a log score over the emitted class probabilities, a proper scoring rule. Each class's log loss is averaged over that class's objects and weighted, 2 for rare or interesting classes and 1 for the rest, so each class counts roughly equally.
  > Submissions are evaluated using a weighted multi-class logarithmic loss
- `designed_for_subjects` = domain-specialist-model · [S4][plasticc-s4]
  - why: Entrants are classifiers trained from scratch on the challenge's labelled light curves for a task astronomy defines, mostly gradient-boosted trees and neural networks, often in ensembles. ### 2.6 CMT-Benchmark (cmt-benchmark)

`data/benchmarks/physics/cmt-benchmark.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-11-18

*Fifty expert-written condensed-matter theory problems for language models, graded by SymPy and numeric checks.*

Fifty original research-level problems in condensed matter theory, written and cross-checked by an international panel of condensed-matter theorists to test whether a language model could work as a research assistant. The problems span Hartree-Fock, exact diagonalization, the density matrix renormalization group, quantum and variational Monte Carlo, projected entangled pair states, statistical mechanics and model building. Authors wrote them in a shared Google Sheet whose extension ran each draft through Gemini 2.0 Flash, 2.5 Flash, 2.5 Pro and GPT-4o, and a problem was accepted only once every one of those models failed it and another author had checked it. A model answers closed-book with a final boxed LaTeX expression: numbers, lettered options, an algebraic expression or an expression in fermionic operators, which the grader reduces to normal order. Each answer is right or wrong, with no partial credit, and the paper reports Pass@1; GPT-5 solved 30% and the mean over 17 models was 11.4%. The problems and answers are public on Hugging Face under MIT. A September 2026 audit by other physicists found errors in 30 of the 50 problems and repaired 29, and Epoch AI rated v1.0.0 Flawed on it; the authors fixed ten problems in v2.0.0 and dispute most of the others as unstated conventions of the subfield.

**Evidence** (33 quoted fields), by checklist area:

#### cmt-benchmark · Identity and id

- `self_description` · [S1][cmt-benchmark-s1]
  > we present CMT-Benchmark, a dataset of 50 original problems covering condensed matter theory (CMT) at the level of an expert researcher
- `released` = 2025-10-06 · [S2][cmt-benchmark-s2]
  > Submitted on 6 Oct 2025
- `release_venue` = ICLR 2026 · [S2][cmt-benchmark-s2]
  > International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR) main conference 2026

#### cmt-benchmark · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary physics/condensed-matter; secondary physics/physics-reasoning · [S1][cmt-benchmark-s1]
  - why: Every problem is condensed matter theory, asking for properties of lattice models of interacting electrons and spins (ground-state energies and degeneracies, order parameters, Goldstone modes, Fermi-surface topology, phase behaviour) or for judgements about the methods that compute them, so the subject is the condensed-matter leaf's. The problems are posed in text and scored on the answer with no simulation in the loop, the secondary leaf's case; CritPt takes that leaf as primary because its problems span most of physics.
  > The solution for these problems involve analytical and computational approaches commonly used in quantum many-body physics and classical statistical mechanics
- `capability` = quantitative-reasoning · [S1][cmt-benchmark-s1]
  - why: Most answers are numbers, algebraic expressions or operator expressions the model must derive, graded by value or by equivalence rather than by prose.
  > We designed problems in multiple answer formats that can be automatically graded, including multiple-choice, numerical values, algebraic expressions, and non-commutative operator expressions
- `evaluation_method` = symbolic-equivalence, numeric-tolerance-match · S3
  - why: The released evaluator decides operator and function answers by simplifying the difference from the reference in SymPy, after reducing fermionic operators to normal order, and accepts numeric answers within a relative tolerance of 1e-6.
  > equivalent \*= np.allclose(model\_element, solution\_element, rtol=1e-6, atol=1e-12)
- `designed_for_subjects` = instruction-tuned-model · [S1][cmt-benchmark-s1]
  - why: A general-purpose model is prompted directly, closed-book and without tools, with the author's prompt and fixed formatting instructions, and its last boxed expression is graded. The 17 models include reasoning models (GPT-5, o3, o4-mini), but no reasoning-effort setting is part of the protocol.
  > Each model is queried with the prompt written by the author, along with a fixed component specifying formatting instructions

Considered and rejected:

- `capability` not `adversarial-robustness` · [S1][cmt-benchmark-s1]
  - why: Problems were kept only if every model on the authors' sheet failed them, which is adversarial filtering of items, but the score is correctness, not a system's resistance to inputs an attacker selects against it.
  > When a problem fails every model available on the sheet, another author would review the problem and solution for correctness before the problem was accepted into the final benchmark dataset.
- `evaluation_method` not `multiple-choice` · [S1][cmt-benchmark-s1]
  - why: Some problems ask for one or more of several lettered options (over five for most), but the options differ by problem, several may be right and no chance baseline is stated, and the headline mixes them with free-form answers, as humanitys-last-exam's near miss reads.
  > we ask for one or more choices from among many options (over 5 for most problems)
- `evaluation_method` not `model-graded-judge` · [S4][cmt-benchmark-s4]
  - why: Only the September 2026 audit grades with an LLM judge (as\_used); the benchmark's own grader is programmatic.
  > CMT-Benchmark has no public evaluator, so we adapt the HLE evaluation pipeline, including its system prompt and LLM-judge prompt, to assess responses against the provided reference solutions.
- `evaluation_method` not `human-expert-eval` · [S1][cmt-benchmark-s1]
  - why: The authors hand-graded the few problems their parser failed on, a fallback rather than the scoring method (see reproducibility\_tier).
  > The parser failed for a small number of problems, which were human-graded.
- `designed_for_subjects` not `tool-augmented-model` · [S4][cmt-benchmark-s4]
  - why: The protocol offers no tools. The September 2026 audit ran two of its three models with tools (as\_used), which is a condition of those results, not the design.
  > use Codex and Claude Code, respectively, with tools enabled

#### cmt-benchmark · Task and evaluation

- `learned_entrant_evidence` = system GPT-5 · [S1][cmt-benchmark-s1]
  > The best performing models were GPT-5 (30.0%), GPT-o3 (26.0%), and GPT-5-mini (24.0%)
- `reproducible_by_third_party` = true · [S1][cmt-benchmark-s1]
  - why: The problems, the reference answers and the evaluator are public, so anyone can query a model and grade it; a response the parser cannot read needs a condensed-matter expert to grade, as the authors did.
  > Our dataset can be found in the Hugging Face repository
- `task` = exists true; input one condensed-matter theory problem stated in text, with the parameters, variables and functions its answer may use, and fixed formatting instructions; output A final answer in a boxed LaTeX expression, which may be one or more numbers, a choice of lettered options, an algebraic expression or an expression in non-commuting operators. Only the last boxed expression is graded; the reasoning before it is discarded.; scoring Pass@1 over the 50 problems, each correct or incorrect against the author's answer with no partial credit, by a LaTeX-to-SymPy parser (evaluation\_method\_note); problems the parser failed on were graded by hand. · [S1][cmt-benchmark-s1]
  > We then verify equivalence using standard Sympy symbolic equivalence checks
- `execution.reproducibility_tier` = requires-human-raters · [S1][cmt-benchmark-s1]

### 2.7 QCircuitBench (qcircuitbench)

`data/benchmarks/physics/qcircuitbench.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-10-14

*Quantum algorithm design as code generation: LLMs write OpenQASM circuits for 25 algorithms, verified by simulation.*

A benchmark and dataset for language models that design and implement quantum algorithms as code. A problem description in natural language and LaTeX names an oracle to construct, a problem to solve with an oracle supplied as a black-box OpenQASM gate, or a quantum state to reproduce. The model answers with an OpenQASM 3.0 circuit and, for algorithm design, a Python post-processing function that runs the circuit on Qiskit's Aer simulator and returns the answer. Three task suites cover 25 algorithms in 120,290 data points: oracle construction (35,872), quantum algorithm design (6,534, from Bernstein-Vazirani and Grover to Shor, the generalized Simon problem and variational algorithms such as VQE and QAOA) and random circuit synthesis over Clifford and universal gate sets (77,884). Verification functions check the QASM and Python syntax and score the semantics by simulation, as the success rate over test oracles and shots or as the fidelity to the target state; BLEU, byte perplexity and gate, shot and time ratios to the reference implementation are reported beside them. A Cirq version mirrors the Qiskit one.

#### qcircuitbench · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary physics/quantum-systems; secondary code/function-synthesis · [S2][qcircuitbench-s2]
  - why: The subject is quantum circuits, which the leaf names, and every semantic score is a property of a simulated quantum process, the outcome statistics of a circuit run on Qiskit's simulator or the fidelity of the state it prepares. ADR-0017's cross-over ruling puts a quantum (machine-learning) algorithm benchmark with a model-shaped subject in physics/quantum-systems. The code family's inclusion test also passes, since the model writes a program that tests run, so function synthesis is secondary; physics is primary because the code family excludes code that is the means to a result in another field (review\_checks).
  > we run the quantum circuit simulation for a number of shots
- `capability` = generation-fidelity · [S2][qcircuitbench-s2]
  - why: The largest suite, random circuit synthesis (77,884 of the 120,290 data points), and the state-preparation tasks score the generated circuit by the fidelity of the state it prepares to the target state, a continuous closeness to a stated specification. The oracle and algorithm tasks score discrete answers against a key, which the term excludes.
  > the semantic score is defined as the fidelity between the generated and target quantum states
- `evaluation_method` = execution-tests, domain-metric, reference-metric · [S2][qcircuitbench-s2]
  - why: The generated circuit and post-processing code are run on Qiskit's Aer simulator against test oracles, and the semantic score is the success rate over test cases and shots (execution-tests). For state preparation and random circuits the score is quantum state fidelity, a measure with no meaning outside quantum information (domain-metric). BLEU against the reference code and byte perplexity are reported for every suite, with gate, shot and time counts as ratios to the reference implementation (reference-metric).
  > we use a suite of end-to-end test cases to validate the functional correctness of the generated circuits
- `designed_for_subjects` = instruction-tuned-model, base-model · [S2][qcircuitbench-s2]
  - why: The paper prompts language models with a problem description after 1 or 5 in-context examples, single-turn and without tools. GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-05-13) answers as an assistant. Meta-Llama-3-8B and Qwen2.5-7B are named by their base checkpoints, and byte perplexity, reported for the open models, scores raw continuation; the README runs the tasks through lm\_eval with a few-shot setting.

**Open review checks** (9):

1. (field `domain`) Domain primary is physics/quantum-systems with code/function-synthesis secondary. The code family's inclusion test passes too (the model writes a program that tests run), and SciCode's entry puts the same shape, science problems solved as tested code, under code primary. The call here rests on the quantum-systems leaf naming circuits, ADR-0017's cross-over ruling and the code family's exclusion of code as the means to a result in another field. · [S2][qcircuitbench-s2]
   > we make a change of perspective by formulating quantum algorithm design as quantum code generation
2. (field `designed_for_subjects`) base-model rests on the open models being named by their base checkpoints (Meta-Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B) and on byte perplexity scoring continuation; the paper does not say whether instruct variants were run. reasoning-model and tool-augmented-model were rejected (no reasoning budget; web search only in an appendix probe).
3. (field `observed_subjects`) Messier (2026) ran five agents in the OpenHands scaffold through Harbor, recorded under as\_used. Whether observed\_subjects should add agent-scaffold, on one paper's evidence. · [S5][qcircuitbench-s5]
   > Each (agent, task) pair was run once.
4. (field `capability`) generation-fidelity rests on the fidelity-scored suites (random circuits and state preparation); the oracle and algorithm-design suites have no capability term, and leaving the facet empty as HumanEval's entry does is the alternative.
5. (field `execution.reproducibility_tier`) reproducibility fully-automatable and compute api-credits-only treat Qiskit's Aer simulator as part of the test runtime. If a quantum circuit simulator counts as a specific simulation environment, both become automatable-with-simulator and simulator-required.
6. (field `governance.maintainer_type`) maintainer\_type individual because the repository sits in a personal GitHub account; the authors are a Peking University group, and academic-lab applies if an institution is held to be the holder (the Dataverse deposit's holder was not read).
7. (field `data.ceiling_anchor_type`) ceiling\_anchor\_type left null. The human study's participants and instructions are in Figure 12, an image whose text the PDF does not carry; reading it would settle crowd-average or expert-average. · [S2][qcircuitbench-s2]
   > we conduct a human study and report human baseline scores at the bottom line of each table as reference
8. (field `versions`) No versions are recorded. arXiv v1 (QCircuitNet, 2024) predates the three-suite, 25-algorithm set and evaluated other models; its PDF was not read, so whether v1 is a breaking edition, and what it held, is open. The entry treats QCircuitNet as the same benchmark. · [S1][qcircuitbench-s1]
   > we introduce QCircuitNet, the first benchmark and test dataset designed to evaluate AI
9. (field `data.access`) access fully-open rests on the paper and README; the full dataset's Google Drive link and the Harvard Dataverse deposit were not fetched.

### 2.8 SRBench (srbench)

`data/benchmarks/physics/srbench.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-10-14

*Living benchmark of symbolic regression methods: R^2 and model size on PMLB data, and recovery of known physics laws.*

A living benchmark for symbolic regression (SR), the search for a closed-form expression that fits a dataset, kept by a lab at Boston Children's Hospital and Harvard Medical School with method contributions from the SR community. Every method is wrapped behind a scikit-learn API, refitted from scratch on each dataset's training split and must return its model as a sympy-compatible string. The benchmark has two halves. A black-box track scores test-set R^2 and model size on tabular regression problems from PMLB, real-world and synthetic, against machine-learning regressors in v2.0. A ground-truth track gives data generated from known equations: in v2.0 (NeurIPS 2021) 130 problems from the Feynman Lectures on Physics and from Strogatz's nonlinear ODE systems, scored by the symbolic solution rate at four levels of target noise; in SRBench 2025, 12 phenomenological and first-principles problems (Hubble, Kepler, Planck and others), compared with the known expression on accuracy-size Pareto fronts. v2.0 ran 14 SR and 7 ML methods on 252 problems; SRBench 2025 ran 25 SR methods in Docker containers, 30 runs per dataset, on 24 datasets. Contributors submit methods by pull request and the maintainers run them in the next update.

#### srbench · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary physics/symbolic-regression-discovery · [S2][srbench-s2]
  - why: The ground-truth track asks methods to recover the equations of physical systems (Feynman Lectures equations, Strogatz ODEs; in 2025 laws such as Hubble's, Kepler's and Planck's) from data, which is the subdomain's definition. The black-box half is tabular regression from health, business, government and other fields and meets no domain in the vocabulary (review\_checks).
  > These datasets were used to assess the ability of SR methods to recover known process physics.
- `capability` = inductive-reasoning · [S2][srbench-s2]
  - why: Each method gets a finite set of observations and is scored on the expression it infers from them, on held-out data and, for the ground-truth problems, on whether it is the generating law.
  > the Symbolic Solution metric is a more faithful evaluation of the ability of an SR method to discover the data generating process
- `evaluation_method` = statistical-fit, symbolic-equivalence · [S2][srbench-s2]
  - why: Accuracy in v2.0 and 2025 is the coefficient of determination R^2 on a held-out 25% test split (statistical-fit). In v2.0 a ground-truth model counts as solved when, after sympy simplification, it differs from the true equation by an additive constant or a scalar factor (symbolic-equivalence). Model size, the axis paired with R^2 throughout, is a reporting axis, not a method (ADR-0020).
  > is designed to capture models that differ from the true model by a constant or scalar
- `designed_for_subjects` = task-specific-supervised-model · [S2][srbench-s2]
  - why: The entrants are fitting procedures (genetic programming, Bayesian and deep-learning SR, pretrained transformers and, in v2.0, ML regressors for comparison) refitted on every dataset's training split, which the term's inclusion test names for symbolic regression.
  > Each algorithm was trained on each dataset (and level of noise, for ground-truth problems) in 10 repeated trials
- `secondary_axes` = energy · [S5][srbench-s5]
  > Additionally, we analyze trade-offs between model complexity, accuracy, and energy consumption.

SRBench 2025 could be an entry of its own. · [S5][srbench-s5]

Both tests send symbolic regression to task-specific-supervised-model; classical-algorithm's exclusion names it. No edition has a language-model-based method.

### 2.9 Fusion Equilibrium Challenge (fusion-equilibrium-challenge)

`data/benchmarks/physics/fusion-equilibrium-challenge.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-10-14

*Tokamak equilibrium reconstruction without magnetic sensors: DIII-D flux maps, then zero-shot transfer to MAST.*

A NeurIPS 2026 competition, run by Sophelio with General Atomics and the University of Texas at Austin, on shots from two tokamaks: DIII-D (General Atomics) and MAST (UKAEA). From a shot's coil currents, plasma current and Thomson-scattering electron temperature and density profiles, with no magnetic diagnostics, a model predicts at every EFIT timestep the 65x65 poloidal flux map psi(R,Z) and the two scalars a flux map cannot contain, q95 and betaN. The scorer derives the plasma boundary and seven shape scalars from the submitted flux with the same code it applies to EFIT's reconstruction, which is the ground truth. Challenge 1 ranks S\_model on DIII-D, a weighted blend of R2 on psi, R2 on q95 and betaN, a normalised Hausdorff distance between boundaries and the agreement of the derived scalars. Challenge 2 ranks G\_ratio, the MAST score over the DIII-D score, for a model given no MAST training data. Training shots and test inputs are on Hugging Face under CC BY 4.0; the targets are withheld and scored on Codabench, in a development phase on a public test fold (2026-07-27 to 2026-10-18) and a blind final phase on private folds (2026-10-19 to 2026-10-26), with results due at NeurIPS in December 2026.

#### fusion-equilibrium-challenge · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary physics/plasma-fusion · [S1][fusion-equilibrium-challenge-s1]
  - why: The scored quantity is the magnetic equilibrium of a tokamak plasma, inferred from two machines' diagnostics, which is the leaf's definition (predicting plasma behaviour in fusion devices).
  > reconstruct the two-dimensional poloidal flux function ψ(R, Z) and a suite of scalar equilibrium parameters from non-magnetic diagnostics alone
- `capability` = scientific-prediction · [S1][fusion-equilibrium-challenge-s1]
  - why: A model predicts the state of a physical system, the plasma's flux map and two scalars, from measurements of it, and is scored against a reference computation, EFIT's reconstruction.
  > Given the non-magnetic diagnostic inputs at all EFIT timestamps of a held-out shot, predict the full 65 × 65 poloidal flux map
- `capability` = distribution-shift-generalization · [S1][fusion-equilibrium-challenge-s1]
  - why: Challenge 2 trains on DIII-D and scores zero-shot on MAST, a spherical tokamak with another coil set, and reports that score as its own condition beside the DIII-D one. The task and targets are unchanged and only the machine moves, so the shift term applies rather than transfer-learning, whatever the source calls it; taxonomy/capabilities.yaml names this benchmark as the term's example.
  > Two complementary awards reward intra-machine reconstruction fidelity (Smodel) on DIII-D and zero-shot cross-machine generalization (Gratio) to the topologically distinct MAST spherical tokamak
- `evaluation_method` = composite, statistical-fit · [S1][fusion-equilibrium-challenge-s1]
  - why: S\_model is a fixed weighted sum of four terms: pooled R2 on the flux map, pooled R2 on q95 and betaN, one minus a length-normalised Hausdorff distance between predicted and reference boundaries, and the mean R2 of seven scalars derived from the flux. Each is an error against EFIT's reference, so statistical-fit is the constituent method; composite records that the headline blends different metrics. G\_ratio, Challenge 2's ranking, is a ratio of two S\_model values.
  > with organizer-default weights (w1, w2, w3, w4) = (0.55, 0.15, 0.10, 0.20) summing to 1
- `designed_for_subjects` = scientific-surrogate-model · [S2][fusion-equilibrium-challenge-s2]
  - why: The entrant stands in for EFIT with its magnetic measurements and is scored against what EFIT produced, which is the term's inclusion test. Any method is admitted, from ridge regression to neural operators.
  > A single learned mapping turns coil currents and laser profiles into the flux surfaces, plasma boundary, and equilibrium parameters EFIT normally derives from magnetic sensors.

Considered and rejected:

- `evaluation_method` not `domain-metric` · [S1][fusion-equilibrium-challenge-s1]
  - why: D\_LCFS is specific to plasma boundaries, but it is the challenge's own normalisation of a general Hausdorff distance, not a metric named and standardised within the discipline.
  > A length-normalized symmetric Hausdorff distance
- `designed_for_subjects` not `classical-algorithm` · [S2][fusion-equilibrium-challenge-s2]
  - why: Physics-based pipelines are allowed, and the rules let entrants train on synthetic equilibria from their own free-boundary solvers, but the challenge is built for learned mappings and its four reference baselines are all learned.
  > No restriction on language or framework — from ridge regression to neural operators.

The abstract has 9,113 DIII-D and 2,416 MAST (the README's 9,113 "source shots", before the diverted-plasma filter); the paper body 8,794 and 2,414 (all folds); the site 7,915 and 1,206 (the released folds); the 2026-10-09 announcement 879 and 1,205 private shots, which give 2,411 MAST, not 2,414. · [S6][fusion-equilibrium-challenge-s6]
   > validated to make the correct, unambiguous call on all 9,113 DIII-D source shots
4. (field `execution.reproducibility_tier`) The paper says the private fold's ground truth stays confidential until the end of Phase 2; Codabench's rules and terms say it is never released. If the targets are released after the final phase, reproducibility\_tier and the private-test-set blocker change for later use. · [S1][fusion-equilibrium-challenge-s1]
   > remain confidential until the end of Phase 2
5. (field `activity`) activity reads closed: a one-off competition whose final results are published. Re-read after the December 2026 NeurIPS session; lifecycle may read mature then.
6. (field `execution.harness_availability`) official-harness rests on the starter kit's fusion\_scoring/ being the scorer's own modules, run locally on held-out training shots. The README also says the scorer itself is not in the kit, which could read as reference-implementation-only. · [S6][fusion-equilibrium-challenge-s6]
   > The scorer runs on Codabench against held-out ground truth; it is not part of this starter kit.
7. (field `governance.independence_flags`) No source names who funds the two $500 awards, so prize-sponsored-by-industry is unset. Sophelio is a company and runs the challenge, and the paper says no external sponsor is needed. · [S1][fusion-equilibrium-challenge-s1]
   > no external sponsor is required to run the challenge.
8. (field `designed_for_subjects`) Some development entries look physics-based (one fact-sheet method name describes a Green's-function flux model for MAST), so observed\_subjects might add classical-algorithm. The leaderboard was not made a Source because its rows carry personal account names.
9. (field `ground_truth_source`) ground\_truth\_source is held-out-labels; simulation is the other reading, since the labels are a physics code's reconstruction fitted to measurements.

### 2.10 CritPt (critpt)

`data/benchmarks/physics/critpt.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-05 · last verified 2026-11-18

*Unpublished, research-level physics challenges with machine-checkable answers, graded on a private test set.*

Seventy-one research-scale physics challenges, written by more than fifty active researchers from their own unpublished work across condensed matter, quantum, atomic and optical, high-energy, astro- and statistical physics and more, each with a guess-resistant answer -- a number, a symbolic expression or a composite of them -- that an automated pipeline grades. The challenges are also split into 190 smaller checkpoints. One challenge is public as an example; the answers to the other seventy are private, and models are scored through the maintainers' online grading server.

**Evidence** (21 quoted fields), by checklist area:

#### critpt · Identity and id

- `self_description` · [S1][critpt-s1]
  > the first benchmark designed to test LLMs on unpublished, research-level reasoning tasks that broadly covers modern physics research areas

#### critpt · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary physics/physics-reasoning · [S1][critpt-s1]
  - why: Physics problems posed in text and scored on the physics answer, with no simulation in the loop -- the leaf's definition -- across most of modern physics.
  > including condensed matter, quantum physics, atomic, molecular & optical physics, astrophysics, high energy physics, mathematical physics, statistical physics, nuclear physics
- `capability` = quantitative-reasoning · [S1][critpt-s1]
  - why: Each challenge ends in a number or symbolic expression the model must derive, graded by value or by symbolic equivalence, not by prose.
  > Every problem is hand-curated to admit a guess-resistant and machine-verifiable answer
- `evaluation_method` = numeric-tolerance-match, symbolic-equivalence · [S1][critpt-s1]
  - why: The grader compares numbers and, for symbolic answers, checks equivalence with SymPy.
  > Symbolic expressions: For problems involving symbolic algebra, we use a hierarchical grading script based on SymPy

#### critpt · Task and evaluation

- `learned_entrant_evidence` = system GPT-5 (high, code & web) · [S1][critpt-s1]
  > GPT-5 (high, code & web) 12.6 21.4 24.5 10.0 14.4 17.6
- `reproducible_by_third_party` = true · [S1][critpt-s1]
  - why: Anyone can score a model through the public pipeline and grading server; nobody outside the maintainers can grade without it, since the answers are private.
  > enabling independent validation and continual monitoring of frontier model progress
- `task` = exists true; input one research challenge stated in text, with its symbols, conventions and units; output A final answer -- a number, a symbolic expression or a composite of them -- in a fixed template, produced in a second, formatting turn after the solving turn.; scoring Accuracy over the seventy test challenges, averaged over five independent runs per model; graded automatically against the expert answer.; tests_hidden_from_system true · [S1][critpt-s1]
  > To disentangle the reasoning process from answer formatting, we adopt a two-step generation strategy
- `execution.compute_tier` = api-credits-only · [S1][critpt-s1]
  - why: Models are called through their providers' APIs and graded by script; the paper reports the cost of each run in API spend.

#### critpt · Data and licence

- `as_used` = protocol An expert audit's re-grading. Specialists reviewed 56 of the 70 test challenges, repaired 19 and excluded 2, and derived their own reference solutions, since the official ones are private; models were then scored against those as mean@4 and pass@4 over four attempts, GPT-5.6-Sol and Fable 5 with tools (Codex, Claude Code) and Gemini 3.1 Pro without. The pre-audit numbers it sets beside them are Artificial Analysis's mean@5 on all 70, from the grading server.; split v1, the 54 test challenges the audit retained (19 of them repaired) · [S2][critpt-s2]

**Open review checks** (4):

1. contamination\_risk low rests on the problems being unpublished and the answers private; no contamination study is cited, and low needs none.
2. reproducibility not-independently-reproducible because only the maintainers can grade; a reviewer who reads the grading server as a third-party route may prefer fully-automatable.
3. (field `governance.known_limitation`) The Flawed verdict and both audits are of v1, and the paper's scores the entry carries (learned\_entrant\_evidence, the tool comparison in the header) are v1 scores from before either audit. v2 revised 47 challenges and has not been reviewed, so whether the defects persist in v2 is unknown; the verdict is recorded as a known limitation, not as a change to any facet. · [S3][critpt-s3]
   > We reviewed v1. As of October 22, 2026, the leaderboard reports v2. v2 revised 47 challenges, full details are available at the latest commit.
4. (field `data.ceiling_anchor_type`) The audit's corrected set (54 challenges, the audit's own reference answers) puts one model's pass@4 at 94.44%, close to the ceiling, where the grading server's v1 scores stayed near a third. Saturation is computed from claims (12 S4), and the corrected set is not the benchmark's, but it bears on whether the 70-challenge test set measures what it claims and on ceiling\_anchor\_type's solvable-by-construction basis. · [S2][critpt-s2]
   > On the corrected set, GPT-5.6-Sol Max achieves a mean@4 of 87.50% and a pass@4 of 94.44%.
